claims.text: The Enabling Act of 1933 was passed by the Reichstag on 23 March 1933 with a two-thirds majority. The Nazis and their ally the DNVP controlled well below two-thirds of the votes. The Communist delegates had been banned from participation. The Nazis used intimidation tactics, such as surrounding the Reichstag with SA members, to secure the necessary votes. The Nazis promised religious freedom to the Catholic Centre Party to secure the necessary votes. Only the Social Democratic Party (SPD) voted in opposition to the Enabling Act. The vote on the Enabling Act was 444 to 94. The Reichstag president Hermann Göring changed the rules of procedure to reduce the quorum required for constitutional amendments. Hermann Göring did not count the 81 absent Communist deputies in the quorum calculation. The quorum was lowered from 432 to 378. The Nazis used coercion, bribery, and manipulation of parliamentarians to ensure the bill's passage. Communist and some Social Democrat deputies had already been arrested under the Reichstag Fire Decree.
claims.reason: "When the newly-elected Reichstag convenednot including the Communist delegates whose participation in politics had been bannedit passed the Enabling Act (23 March 1933)." - all details about vote, intimidation, bans, and tactics are supported in sources.

claims.text: Operation Sea Lion was never launched after the Battle of Britain because Adolf Hitler considered invasion a last resort, to be used only if all other options had failed. The German forces never achieved air and naval superiority over the English Channel and the proposed landing sites. The Luftwaffe suffered mounting losses in the Battle of Britain. There was no sign that the Royal Air Force had been defeated. Adolf Hitler postponed Sea Lion indefinitely on 17 September 1940. The German High Command and Adolf Hitler himself had serious doubts about the prospects for success of Operation Sea Lion. Key figures like Göring doubted the Luftwaffe could win control of the skies. Adolf Galland and Rundstedt believed the invasion plans were not serious or were a bluff to pressure the British government. Most historians agree that the German Kriegsmarine's weakness compared to the Royal Navy would have made the invasion a disaster. The weakness of the German Kriegsmarine compared to the Royal Navy further discouraged the execution of Operation Sea Lion.
